newsitem.title: USA: Aon still interested in acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: Aon still interested in acquisitions.

text.p: Aon Corp, the big Chicago-based insurance broker that has purchased three of its rivals in the last six months, said it was still interested in doing more deals.

But Aon chief executive Patrick Ryan, in a telephone interview with Reuters, declined to comment on whether he would consider making an offer for U.K. brokers Willis Corroon Group Plc or Sedgwick Group Plc.
"We've got a lot that we're doing right now," he said. "They're both fine companies. I don't know what their future is. But we don't discuss individual companies," he said.

The future of Willis Corroon and Sedgwick has been the subject of much speculation in recent weeks following a wave of consolidation in the insurance brokerage industry that has put them far behind industry giants Aon and Marsh & McLennan Cos Inc.

And Aon, which bought Bain Hogg Group Plc in October, Alexander & Alexander Services Inc in January and agreed to buy Minet Group in April, has proven to be a major force in the industry's consolidation.
Marsh & McLennan's agreement to buy privately-held Johnson & Higgins further increased the pressure on Willis and Sedgwick.
Although Aon's buying spree took a toll on results for the first quarter of 1997, Ryan said he expects to achieve cost savings of $240-$250 million from the merged businesses by 1998.
And those cost savings should lead to a "fairly nice contribution to earnings," Ryan said.
However, Ryan declined to estimate how much of a contribution to earnings he expects from those businesses.
Aon on Thursday reported a first-quarter net loss of $0.02 a share compared with a profit of $0.69 a year ago.
Those results included special charges of $0.54 after-tax, most of which were connected to the Alexander & Alexander acquisition.
First-quarter operating earnings, before the special charges were $0.51 a share compared with $0.56 a year ago.

Although Aon has a lot on its table with the acquisitions of Alexander & Alexander, Bain Hogg and Minet, Ryan said the company was capable of doing still more deals in the insurance broking or consulting industries.

The company, he said, is an experienced consolidator accustomed to doing a large number of deals and said some branches of the business will not be involved with the integration of these latest deals and therefore will be free to tackle other projects.
"We've been doing acquisitions pretty aggressively for the last decade," Ryan said.
"So we'll continue to make acquisitions as part of our strategy to have organic growth coupled with acquisitions," he said.

Aon in October spent about $250 million to buy Bain Hogg, the eleventh-largest broker in the world, and then two months later agreed to spend about $1.23 billion to buy Alexander & Alexander, the fourth-largest insurance broker in the world.
Future deals could be "boutiques that are digested by a part of the company that has very little other activity being digested at the time," he said.

"It's not a matter of overall capacity, it's more a matter of capacity to take on in the area that you are acquiring," he said. "In certain parts of the Aon world, there's nothing being integrated," he said.
"We constantly have deals that we're discussing with people," he said.
Meanwhile, Ryan said he sees the company's growth coming from a number of areas.
"We think there's strong growth internationally, we think there's strong growth in the service side of the business," he said.

"We think there's certainly opportunity for market share increase in broking itself or reinsurance broking, but a lot of the growth will come from the expansion of services, many of them services that get exported around the world in this very large distribution network we have," he said.
